description: Yemayá is the Yoruba orisha of the sea, motherhood, and fish, brought to Cuba through the transatlantic slave trade. In Santería she owns all waters, governs maternity and fertility, and is syncretized with Our Lady of Regla. She is motherly and protective but destructive when angered, her waters creating rivers and floods.
source: Yoruba religion, Santería (Cuba); snip documented by Lydia Cabrera, Miguel A. De La Torre
research_notes: Well-documented orisha across Yoruba, Cuban, Brazilian traditions. Country/culture correctly Cuba.

description: River Mumma (River Maiden) is a Jamaican water spirit appearing as a beautiful woman with long black hair, comb and mirror, dwelling at river sources. Derived from West African Mami Wata traditions via the Twi Nsuo Ba (river child/virgin). She lures men, grants riches to the favored, and punishes disrespect.
source: Jamaican oral tradition; snip West African Mami Wata diaspora; snip documented in Jamaican folklore collections
research_notes: Attested in Jamaican folklore, linked to Mami Wata. Also called River Maiden from Twi Nsuo Ba.

description: The Rolling Calf is a feared Barbadian and Jamaican duppy (malevolent spirit) taking the form of a headless bull or goat with blazing red eyes, trailing chains, and foul stench. It roams villages at night, chasing and terrifying travelers. A classic duppy variant documented in Caribbean folklore collections.
source: Barbadian and Jamaican duppy folklore; snip National Library of Jamaica collections; snip Martha Warren Beckwith Black Roadways
research_notes: Well-documented duppy variant in Barbados and Jamaica. Country Barbados correct.

description: Rounces are Vincentian spirit-animals causing night terrors by riding sleepers, producing paralysis and oppression. Documented in Saint Vincent and the Grenadines folklore as nocturnal entities that sing and induce sleep paralysis, related to the wider Caribbean duppy/jumbie complex.
source: Saint Vincent and the Grenadines oral tradition; snip Caribbean spirit folklore
research_notes: Attested in Vincentian folklore but limited academic documentation. Related to night-mare spirits across Caribbean.

description: Jumbie (jumbee) is a generic Caribbean term for malevolent spirits of the dead, widespread across Antigua, Barbados, Guyana, and the Lesser Antilles. Derived from Kongo nfumbi (ancestral ghost) and Akan duppy. They shape-shift into animals, haunt silk cotton trees, and are repelled by shoes, salt, or crossing water. Central to Obeah and Montserrat jumbie dances.
source: Caribbean folklore (Antigua, Guyana, Montserrat, Lesser Antilles); snip Elsie Clews Parsons 1918 Bahamian transcripts; snip Kongo nfumbi etymology
research_notes: Well-attested across Caribbean. Country Antigua and Barbuda is one of many; snip term is pan-Caribbean.

description: Jé-rouges (Lougawou) are Haitian werewolf-like shapeshifters from Vodou tradition, capable of transforming into wolves or other animals to hunt at night. They function as familiars for bokors (sorcerers), characterized by red glowing eyes. Documented in Haitian folklore collections by Simpson (1942) and later ethnographies.
source: Haitian Vodou folklore; snip George Eaton Simpson Loup Garou and Loa Tales (1942); snip Haitian oral tradition
research_notes: Attested Haitian werewolf figure. Lougawou is the Creole term; snip Jé-rouges appears as variant spelling.

description: Palo Mayombe is not a spirit but an Afro-Cuban religion (Las Reglas de Congo) derived from Kongo traditions. Its spirits are mpungu (deities like Lucero, Sarabanda, Madre de Agua) and nfumbe (dead spirits housed in nganga vessels). The entry misclassifies a religion as a creature.
source: Afro-Cuban Palo religion; snip ethnographies by Ochoa, Kerestetzi, Fernández Olmos & snip Paravisini-Gebert
research_notes: Entry misclassified: Palo Mayombe is a religion, not a spirit. Its entities are mpungu and nfumbe. Should be removed or reclassified.

description: Culebra de Coamo is a sacred serpent guardian of the Coamo thermal springs in Puerto Rico. Described as a large luminous snake with emerald and gold scales, diamond-patterned spine, and jet eyes. It permits only the pure-hearted to bathe in the healing waters, boiling the springs if disrespected. A distinct Puerto Rican tradition.
source: Puerto Rican oral tradition; snip Coamo hot springs folklore
research_notes: Attested in Puerto Rican folklore specific to Coamo springs. Limited academic documentation but consistent local tradition.

description: The Tokoloshe (Tikoloshe) is a Zulu and Xhosa water spirit — a dwarf-like, hairy creature that becomes invisible by swallowing a stone or drinking water. Created by witch doctors to harm enemies, it causes illness, death, and bites sleepers' toes. Protection involves raising beds on bricks. Documented in Nguni ethnography and contemporary South African belief.
source: Zulu and Xhosa oral tradition; snip Nguni mythology; snip Fordred-Green 2000 Current Anthropology; snip Scholtz Tales of the Tokoloshe
research_notes: Well-attested in Zulu/Xhosa tradition. Country South Africa correct; snip culture Zulu/Xhosa.

description: //Gaunab (Gaunab) is the Khoikhoi malevolent deity of death, sickness, and misfortune, personifying darkness and the west. He eternally battles the creator Tsui-//Goab, who wounded his knees in their wrestling match. The lunar cycle reflects their conflict: waning moon is //Gaunab's temporary victory, new crescent marks Tsui-//Goab's return. Documented by Theophilus Hahn (1881) and later scholars.
source: Theophilus Hahn Tsuni-//Goab (1881); snip Khoikhoi theology; snip Patricia Ann Lynch African Mythology A to Z
research_notes: Well-documented Khoikhoi deity. Correctly attributed to Khoikhoi culture in Namibia. Name uses Khoekhoe click orthography //G.

description: Impundulu (lightning bird, thekwane) is the Zulu and Xhosa vampiric lightning bird — a human-sized black-and-white bird that summons thunder and lightning with wings and talons. It functions as a witch's familiar, drinks blood, can take human form to seduce women, and is passed down matrilineally. Only fire can destroy it. Documented by Berglund, Werner, and contemporary belief.
source: Zulu and Xhosa oral tradition; snip Axel-Ivar Berglund Zulu Thought-Patterns (1975); snip Alice Werner Myths and Legends of the Bantu (1933)
research_notes: Well-attested Zulu/Xhosa lightning bird. Country South Africa correct; snip culture Zulu/Xhosa.

description: Inkanyamba is a Zulu and Xhosa serpentine water spirit associated with Howick Falls (Umgeni River, KwaZulu-Natal). Its name means "snake cloud" — it causes tornadoes and seasonal storms. Described as a multi-headed serpent with horselike head, dorsal fins, and fish tail. Appeased for rain and fertility; snip angered by corrugated roofs mimicking water.
source: Zulu and Xhosa oral tradition; snip Felicity Wood Critical Arts (2000); snip Michael Newton Encyclopedia of Cryptozoology; snip Jan Knappert African Mythology
research_notes: Well-attested in Zulu/Xhosa tradition around Howick Falls. Country Eswatini in record is incorrect — primary locus is KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa.

description: The Grey Crowned Crane is Zimbabwe's national bird and holds cultural significance in Shona tradition as a messenger between the living and ancestors (midzimu) on the granite hills. While not a formal deity, crane spirits appear in Shona cosmology as intermediaries carrying prayers to Mwari. The specific named entity lacks direct ethnographic citation but draws on attested avian symbolism.
source: Shona cosmology (Bourdillon, Gelfand); snip crowned crane as national bird and ancestral messenger; snip avian symbolism in midzimu veneration
research_notes: Partially attested: crowned crane is culturally significant in Shona Zimbabwe as ancestral messenger, but "Crane Spirit of Shona" as a named entity is not directly documented. Culture Zimbabwe correct.

description: Zimwi is a Shona ogre (giant, hairy, man-eating) from Zimbabwe folklore, dwelling in forests and caves. It represents the danger of wilderness and strangers, often depicted with backwards feet to confuse trackers. Heroes outwit it through cleverness. The term zimwi appears in Bantu religion literature as a class of ogre-like beings across southern Africa (amazimu in Zulu, madimo in Sotho).
source: Shona oral tradition; snip Bantu religion literature (zimwi/madimo/amazimu as ogre class); snip Zimbabwe folklore collections
research_notes: Attested in Shona folklore as ogre. Term zimwi appears in comparative Bantu religion. Country Zimbabwe correct.

description: Zumwani is a Herero water spirit of Namibia, appearing as an exceedingly beautiful woman with reed-like hair wearing colorful cloth, dwelling in rivers, pans, and waterholes. She tests men's character at water's edge: rewarding the respectful with good rains, drowning the disrespectful. Associated with seasonal rains and water scarcity in Herero pastoral culture.
source: Herero oral tradition (Namibia); snip Namibian folklore collections; snip limited academic documentation
research_notes: Attested in Herero tradition of Namibia. Limited academic sources but consistent in Namibian folklore references. Culture correctly Herero/Namibia.

description: Nya-nya Bulembu is a Swazi (Eswatini) monster haunting deep pools, described as a massive moss-green beast with fur like living seaweed. It preys on the careless, transforms victims into monsters, and punishes ritual violations. The name suggests a pool-dwelling entity in siSwati. Limited documentation outside local Swazi folklore references.
